questions.q: A dataset is actively maintained as the authoritative source by a separate vendor platform, and Salesforce only needs current visibility into it. Per this lesson's first question, what does that point toward?
options: A standard custom object with a nightly sync
A Big Object, since external data implies high volume
An External Object, since replicating data already owned elsewhere creates a second copy that will drift
A Custom Metadata Type, since it's not generated by Salesforce
questions.explain: When another system already owns and maintains a dataset as the system of record, replicating it into Salesforce risks drift — the lesson's first question points this toward an External Object rather than a replicated copy.

questions.q: A per-region 'returns window' value needs to be changed directly by store managers without IT involvement or a deployment. Which placement fits, per the configuration-vs-data question in this lesson?
options: A Custom Metadata Type, since configuration should always deploy with releases
A Custom Setting, since it needs to be tunable live, per org/region, without a deployment cycle
A standard custom object with a validation rule
A Big Object indexed on region
questions.explain: A value business users need to tune live, without a deployment, is the Custom Setting case described in this lesson's third question (and detailed in Lesson 10).

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is wrong with the instinct to 'just bring everything into Salesforce'?
options: Nothing — it's always the safest choice
It is only a problem for orgs on Professional Edition
It ignores Salesforce's specific storage economics and performance characteristics at volume, risking skewed owners and un-indexed million-row objects
It only matters for File Storage, not Data Storage
questions.explain: The lesson identifies 'bring everything in' as treating Salesforce as a universal data store rather than a platform with real storage cost and performance tradeoffs at scale, leading to exactly the skew and indexing problems covered earlier in the chapter.

questions.q: A dataset needs native reports, dashboards, Flow automation, and list-view visibility working naturally together, which the lesson calls out as a real cost of placing data elsewhere. What does that argue for?
options: Placing it in an External Object regardless of other factors
Ignoring native feature needs entirely in favor of volume alone
Always defaulting to a Big Object when reports are needed
Weighing the need for native platform features as a real factor favoring a standard or custom object, even if volume or ownership might otherwise suggest another option
questions.explain: The fifth question in this lesson's framework treats native platform feature needs (reports, dashboards, automation, search) as a genuine factor that can outweigh volume or ownership considerations when deciding placement.

questions.q: What is the main point of this lesson's five-question framework, as distinct from treating data placement as instinct?
options: It replaces the need to understand Big Objects or External Objects
It guarantees every dataset should ultimately be placed outside Salesforce
It forces the same structured analysis for every dataset, rather than defaulting to whichever placement instinct the last project reinforced
It is only relevant during initial org setup, not ongoing architecture decisions
questions.explain: The lesson's explicit purpose is to replace ad hoc instinct ('bring everything in' or 'keep everything out') with a repeatable, dataset-specific analysis applied consistently.
